title: Choosing Tenses for Precise Meaning
keyIdea: A verb's tense tells the reader when an action happens and what state it is in. Progressive forms (was cooking, will be watching) show an action in progress at a moment. Perfect forms (had cooked, has lived, will have finished) show an action complete by a moment, and the past perfect marks the earlier of two past events. Conditionals use tense to show how real something is: if it rains, we will; if I were, I would; if we had left, we would have. Keep one tense in a passage unless the time really changes.
familyTip: Read a page of a story together and stop at a verb with had, has or will have. Ask: did this happen before or after the other thing in the sentence? Is it finished? Then try changing one verb, like 'was running' to 'had run', and talk about how the meaning changes.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: read which event came first, pick the verb for a scene, sort conditionals, fix tense slips and build a timeline.

kid: Tense tells your reader when something happens. But it can say more than past, present or future. It can show if an action was still going on, if it was already finished, or if it runs right up to now.

The progressive uses be + -ing. 'At six, Dad was cooking' means the cooking was in progress at six. The perfect uses have, has or had + past participle. 'By six, Dad had cooked' means it was finished before six. 'Zara has lived here for three years' means she still lives here. 'Ben lived in Leeds' means that time is over.

When two things happened in the past, the past perfect marks the earlier one. 'When we arrived, the film had started' means the film began first. Without had, 'the film started' comes after we arrived. Conditionals work the same way: 'If it rains, we will stay in' is real. 'If I were a bird, I would fly' is imagined. 'If we had left earlier, we would have caught the bus' means we did not.

In a story, stay in one tense unless the time really changes. 'She opens the door and smiled' slips. But speech marks are different. In 'I love dogs!' she said, the present is right, because she says it now.
adult: Ages 10 to 11. This matches CCSS ELA L.5.1b to L.5.1d (form and use the perfect tenses; use tense to convey times, sequences, states and conditions; recognise and correct inappropriate shifts) and the Year 5 and 6 grammar in England, including the perfect and progressive forms and the subjunctive in 'If I were'.

The lab has five tasks: read which of two past events came first from the past perfect (in two sentences the earlier event is told last), choose between progressive, perfect and simple forms for six scenes, sort six conditionals into real, imagined now and past unreal, fix two slipped verbs in a past narrative while keeping present-tense speech, and order a mixed-tense paragraph on a timeline.

Common mistakes. Pupils read events in the order they are written instead of from the tense, so 'By the time Ali reached the stop, the bus had gone' looks as if Ali came first. Many use the simple past where the present perfect is needed, or the reverse. Some read 'would have' as something that happened. Others treat every change of tense as an error, including dialogue. Ask: when does this happen, and is it finished?

practice.prompt: 'By the time we got home, the snow had melted.' What happened first?
practice.hint: Find the verb with had. The past perfect marks the earlier event.
practice.explain: 'Had melted' is the past perfect, so the snow melted before we got home, even though it is told second.

practice.prompt: Choose the verb: 'At 9 pm last night, I ___ my book.' (I was halfway through it at 9.)
practice.hint: The action was still going on at that moment. Which form shows in progress?
practice.explain: 'Was reading' is the past progressive: was + -ing shows the reading was in progress at 9 pm. 'Had read' would mean it was already finished.

practice.prompt: Lena joined the swimming club in {y}. It is now 2026 and she is still a member. 'Lena has been a member for ___ years.' Fill in the number.
practice.hint: The present perfect counts from when it began right up to now. Take the start year from 2026.
practice.explain: 2026 − {y} = {=2026-y} years. 'Has been' runs up to now, because she is still a member.

practice.prompt: The train left at 10:{a}. I reached the station at 10:{b}. 'When I arrived, the train had left.' How many minutes earlier did the train leave?
practice.hint: 'Had left' is the earlier event. Take the earlier time from the later time.
practice.explain: {b} − {a} = {=b-a} minutes. The past perfect 'had left' tells you the train went first.

practice.prompt: 'If I had known, I would have helped.' What does this tell you?
choices: I did not know, so I did not help
practice.hint: Had + past participle ... would have: is this real or a past that did not happen?
practice.explain: This is a past that did not happen. I did not know, so I did not help.

pool.prompt: Which sentence shows an action finished before another past action?
choices: Mia had packed her bag before the taxi came.
Mia was packing her bag when the taxi came.
pool.explain: 'Had packed' is the past perfect: the packing was finished before the taxi came. 'Was packing' means it was still going on.

pool.prompt: Which fits best? 'Tom moved to Spain in 2019 and still lives there. Tom ___ in Spain since 2019.'
pool.hint: He still lives there. Which form runs up to now?
pool.explain: 'Has lived' is the present perfect: from 2019 up to now. 'Lived' would mean that time is over.

pool.prompt: Jo had been practising since {a} o'clock. The show began at {b} o'clock. For how many hours had she been practising when it began?
pool.hint: 'Had been practising' runs up to a past moment. Count from the start to that moment.
pool.explain: From {a} o'clock to {b} o'clock is {=b-a} hours. The past perfect progressive shows an action going on up to a past moment.

pool.prompt: Which conditional is about an imagined present?
choices: If I were taller, I would reach it.
If it snows, we will build a snowman.
If she had run, she would have won.
pool.hint: If + past, then would, about now.
pool.explain: 'If I were taller, I would reach it' is imagined: I am not taller. 'Will' is real; 'would have' is a past that did not happen.

pool.prompt: Fix the slip: 'Sam ran to the door and opens it.'
pool.hint: The sentence starts in the past. Keep it there.
pool.explain: 'Ran' is past, so 'opens' should be 'opened'. Changing 'ran' to 'runs' would also clash with the rest of a past story.

pool.prompt: In a past story: '"I am so hungry," said Leo.' Should 'am' change to 'was'?
choices: No, speech can be in the present
pool.hint: Inside speech marks, whose words are they, and when are they said?
pool.explain: Leo says this at that moment, so the present 'am' is right inside speech marks. Only the narrator's verbs stay in the past.

pool.prompt: 'By the time I was {a}, I had learned to swim.' I learned at age {b}. How many years before age {a} did I learn?
pool.hint: The past perfect event comes first. Take the earlier age from the later age.
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} years earlier. 'Had learned' happened before I was {a}.

pool.prompt: 'By Friday I will have finished the book.' When do I finish?
choices: I am still reading on Friday
pool.hint: Will have + past participle: done by that moment.
pool.explain: The future perfect means finished by Friday. If I were still reading, I would say 'I will be reading'.
